//==============================================================
// Copyright © 2020 Intel Corporation
//
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
// =============================================================
//
// Bitonic Sort: this algorithm converts a randomized sequence of numbers into
// a bitonic sequence (two ordered sequences), and then merge these two ordered
// sequences into a ordered sequence. Bitonic sort algorithm is briefly
// described as followed:
//
// - First, it decomposes the randomized sequence of size 2**n into 2**(n-1)
// pairs where each pair consists of 2 consecutive elements. Note that each pair
// is a bitonic sequence.
// - Step 0: for each pair (sequence of size 2), the two elements are swapped so
// that the two consecutive pairs form  a bitonic sequence in increasing order,
// the next two pairs form the second bitonic sequence in decreasing order, the
// next two pairs form the third bitonic sequence in  increasing order, etc, ...
// . At the end of this step, we have 2**(n-1) bitonic sequences of size 2, and
// they follow an order increasing, decreasing, increasing, .., decreasing.
// Thus, they form 2**(n-2) bitonic sequences of size 4.
// - Step 1: for each new 2**(n-2) bitonic sequences of size 4, (each new
// sequence consists of 2 consecutive previous sequences), it swaps the elements
// so that at the end of step 1, we have 2**(n-2) bitonic sequences of size 4,
// and they follow an order: increasing, decreasing, increasing, ...,
// decreasing. Thus, they form 2**(n-3) bitonic sequences of size 8.
// - Same logic applies until we reach the last step.
// - Step n: at this last step, we have one bitonic sequence of size 2**n. The
// elements in the sequence are swapped until we have a sequence in increasing
// order.
//
// In this implementation, a randomized sequence of size 2**n is given (n is a
// positive number). At each stage, a part of step, the host redefines the
// ordered sequenes and sends data to the kernel. The kernel swaps the elements
// accordingly in parallel.
//
#include <math.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>
#include <limits>
#include <omp.h>

void ParallelBitonicSort(int input[], int n) {

  // n: the exponent used to set the array size. Array size = power(2, n)
  int size = pow(2, n);

  // step from 0, 1, 2, ...., n-1
  #pragma omp target data map(tofrom: input[0:size]) 
  {
    auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();

    for (int step = 0; step < n; step++) {
      // for each step s, stage goes s, s-1, ..., 0
      for (int stage = step; stage >= 0; stage--) {
        // In each state, construct a number (num_seq) of bitonic sequences of
        // size seq_len (2, 4, ...) num_seq stores the number of bitonic sequences
        // at each stage. seq_len stores the length of the bitonic sequence at
        // each stage.
        int seq_len = pow(2, stage + 1);
        // Constant used in the kernel: 2**(step-stage).
        int two_power = 1 << (step - stage);

        // Offload the work to kernel.
        #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(256)
        for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
          // Assign the bitonic sequence number.
          int seq_num = i / seq_len;

          // Variable used to identified the swapped element.
          int swapped_ele = -1;

          // Because the elements in the first half in the bitonic
          // sequence may swap with elements in the second half,
          // only the first half of elements in each sequence is
          // required (seq_len/2).
          int h_len = seq_len / 2;

          if (i < (seq_len * seq_num) + h_len) swapped_ele = i + h_len;

          // Check whether increasing or decreasing order.
          int odd = seq_num / two_power;

          // Boolean variable used to determine "increasing" or
          // "decreasing" order.
          bool increasing = ((odd % 2) == 0);

          // Swap the elements in the bitonic sequence if needed
          if (swapped_ele != -1) {
            if (((input[i] > input[swapped_ele]) && increasing) ||
                ((input[i] < input[swapped_ele]) && !increasing)) {
              int temp = input[i];
              input[i] = input[swapped_ele];
              input[swapped_ele] = temp;
            }
          }
        }
      }  // end stage
    } // end step

    auto end = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    auto time = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::nanoseconds>(end - start).count();
    printf("Total kernel execution time: %f (ms)\n", time * 1e-6f);
  }
}

// Loop over the bitonic sequences at each stage in serial.
void SwapElements(int step, int stage, int num_sequence, int seq_len,
                  int *array) {
  for (int seq_num = 0; seq_num < num_sequence; seq_num++) {
    int odd = seq_num / (pow(2, (step - stage)));
    bool increasing = ((odd % 2) == 0);

    int h_len = seq_len / 2;

    // For all elements in a bitonic sequence, swap them if needed
    for (int i = seq_num * seq_len; i < seq_num * seq_len + h_len; i++) {
      int swapped_ele = i + h_len;

      if (((array[i] > array[swapped_ele]) && increasing) ||
          ((array[i] < array[swapped_ele]) && !increasing)) {
        int temp = array[i];
        array[i] = array[swapped_ele];
        array[swapped_ele] = temp;
      }
    }  // end for all elements in a sequence
  }    // end all sequences
}

// Function sorts an array in serial using bitonic sort algorithm. The size of
// the array is indicated by the exponent n: the array size is 2 ** n.
inline void BitonicSort(int a[], int n) {
  // n: the exponent indicating the array size = 2 ** n.

  // step from 0, 1, 2, ...., n-1
  for (int step = 0; step < n; step++) {
    // for each step s, stage goes s, s-1,..., 0
    for (int stage = step; stage >= 0; stage--) {
      // Sequences (same size) are formed at each stage.
      int num_sequence = pow(2, (n - stage - 1));
      // The length of the sequences (2, 4, ...).
      int sequence_len = pow(2, stage + 1);

      SwapElements(step, stage, num_sequence, sequence_len, a);
    }
  }
}

// Function showing the array.
void DisplayArray(int a[], int array_size) {
  for (int i = 0; i < array_size; ++i) std::cout << a[i] << " ";
  std::cout << "\n";
}

void Usage(std::string prog_name, int exponent) {
  std::cout << " Incorrect parameters\n";
  std::cout << " Usage: " << prog_name << " n k \n\n";
  std::cout << " n: Integer exponent presenting the size of the input array. "
               "The number of element in\n";
  std::cout << "    the array must be power of 2 (e.g., 1, 2, 4, ...). Please "
               "enter the corresponding\n";
  std::cout << "    exponent between 0 and " << exponent - 1 << ".\n";
  std::cout << " k: Seed used to generate a random sequence.\n";
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {
  int n, seed, size;
  int exp_max = log2(std::numeric_limits<int>::max());

  // Read parameters.
  try {
    n = std::stoi(argv[1]);

    // Verify the boundary of acceptance.
    if (n < 0 || n >= exp_max) {
      Usage(argv[0], exp_max);
      return -1;
    }

    seed = std::stoi(argv[2]);
    size = pow(2, n);
  } catch (...) {
    Usage(argv[0], exp_max);
    return -1;
  }

  std::cout << "\nArray size: " << size << ", seed: " << seed << "\n";

  size_t size_bytes = size * sizeof(int);

  // Memory allocated for host access only.
  int *data_cpu = (int *)malloc(size_bytes);

  // Memory allocated to store gpu results
  int *data_gpu = (int *)malloc(size_bytes);

  // Initialize the array randomly using a seed.
  srand(seed);

  for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
    data_gpu[i] = data_cpu[i] = rand() % 1000;
  }

  std::cout << "Bitonic sort (parallel)..\n";
  ParallelBitonicSort(data_gpu, n);

  std::cout << "Bitonic sort (serial)..\n";
  BitonicSort(data_cpu, n);

  // Verify
  int unequal = memcmp(data_gpu, data_cpu, size_bytes);
  std::cout << (unequal ? "FAIL" : "PASS") << std::endl;

  // Clean CPU memory.
  free(data_cpu);
  free(data_gpu);

  return 0;
}

//==============================================================
// Copyright © 2020 Intel Corporation

// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
// =============================================================
//
// Bitonic Sort: this algorithm converts a randomized sequence of numbers into
// a bitonic sequence (two ordered sequences), and then merge these two ordered
// sequences into a ordered sequence. Bitonic sort algorithm is briefly
// described as followed:
//
// - First, it decomposes the randomized sequence of size 2**n into 2**(n-1)
// pairs where each pair consists of 2 consecutive elements. Note that each pair
// is a bitonic sequence.
// - Step 0: for each pair (sequence of size 2), the two elements are swapped so
// that the two consecutive pairs form  a bitonic sequence in increasing order,
// the next two pairs form the second bitonic sequence in decreasing order, the
// next two pairs form the third bitonic sequence in  increasing order, etc, ...
// . At the end of this step, we have 2**(n-1) bitonic sequences of size 2, and
// they follow an order increasing, decreasing, increasing, .., decreasing.
// Thus, they form 2**(n-2) bitonic sequences of size 4.
// - Step 1: for each new 2**(n-2) bitonic sequences of size 4, (each new
// sequence consists of 2 consecutive previous sequences), it swaps the elements
// so that at the end of step 1, we have 2**(n-2) bitonic sequences of size 4,
// and they follow an order: increasing, decreasing, increasing, ...,
// decreasing. Thus, they form 2**(n-3) bitonic sequences of size 8.
// - Same logic applies until we reach the last step.
// - Step n: at this last step, we have one bitonic sequence of size 2**n. The
// elements in the sequence are swapped until we have a sequence in increasing
// order.
//
// In this implementation, a randomized sequence of size 2**n is given (n is a
// positive number). At each stage, a part of step, the host redefines the
// ordered sequenes and sends data to the kernel. The kernel swaps the elements
// accordingly in parallel.
//
#include <math.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>
#include <limits>
#include <omp.h>

void ParallelBitonicSort(int input[], int n) {

  // n: the exponent used to set the array size. Array size = power(2, n)
  int size = pow(2, n);

  // step from 0, 1, 2, ...., n-1
  #pragma omp target data map(tofrom: input[0:size]) 
  {
    auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();

    for (int step = 0; step < n; step++) {
      // for each step s, stage goes s, s-1, ..., 0
      for (int stage = step; stage >= 0; stage--) {
        // In each state, construct a number (num_seq) of bitonic sequences of
        // size seq_len (2, 4, ...) num_seq stores the number of bitonic sequences
        // at each stage. seq_len stores the length of the bitonic sequence at
        // each stage.
        int seq_len = pow(2, stage + 1);
        // Constant used in the kernel: 2**(step-stage).
        int two_power = 1 << (step - stage);

        // Offload the work to kernel.
        #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(256)
        for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
          // Assign the bitonic sequence number.
          int seq_num = i / seq_len;

          // Variable used to identified the swapped element.
          int swapped_ele = -1;

          // Because the elements in the first half in the bitonic
          // sequence may swap with elements in the second half,
          // only the first half of elements in each sequence is
          // required (seq_len/2).
          int h_len = seq_len / 2;

          if (i < (seq_len * seq_num) + h_len) swapped_ele = i + h_len;

          // Check whether increasing or decreasing order.
          int odd = seq_num / two_power;

          // Boolean variable used to determine "increasing" or
          // "decreasing" order.
          bool increasing = ((odd % 2) == 0);

          // Swap the elements in the bitonic sequence if needed
          if (swapped_ele != -1) {
            if (((input[i] > input[swapped_ele]) && increasing) ||
                ((input[i] < input[swapped_ele]) && !increasing)) {
              int temp = input[i];
              input[i] = input[swapped_ele];
              input[swapped_ele] = temp;
            }
          }
        }
      }  // end stage
    } // end step

    auto end = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    auto time = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::nanoseconds>(end - start).count();
    printf("Total kernel execution time: %f (ms)\n", time * 1e-6f);
  }
}

// Loop over the bitonic sequences at each stage in serial.
void SwapElements(int step, int stage, int num_sequence, int seq_len,
                  int *array) {
  for (int seq_num = 0; seq_num < num_sequence; seq_num++) {
    int odd = seq_num / (pow(2, (step - stage)));
    bool increasing = ((odd % 2) == 0);

    int h_len = seq_len / 2;

    // For all elements in a bitonic sequence, swap them if needed
    for (int i = seq_num * seq_len; i < seq_num * seq_len + h_len; i++) {
      int swapped_ele = i + h_len;

      if (((array[i] > array[swapped_ele]) && increasing) ||
          ((array[i] < array[swapped_ele]) && !increasing)) {
        int temp = array[i];
        array[i] = array[swapped_ele];
        array[swapped_ele] = temp;
      }
    }  // end for all elements in a sequence
  }    // end all sequences
}

// Function sorts an array in serial using bitonic sort algorithm. The size of
// the array is indicated by the exponent n: the array size is 2 ** n.
inline void BitonicSort(int a[], int n) {
  // n: the exponent indicating the array size = 2 ** n.

  // step from 0, 1, 2, ...., n-1
  for (int step = 0; step < n; step++) {
    // for each step s, stage goes s, s-1,..., 0
    for (int stage = step; stage >= 0; stage--) {
      // Sequences (same size) are formed at each stage.
      int num_sequence = pow(2, (n - stage - 1));
      // The length of the sequences (2, 4, ...).
      int sequence_len = pow(2, stage + 1);

      SwapElements(step, stage, num_sequence, sequence_len, a);
    }
  }
}

// Function showing the array.
void DisplayArray(int a[], int array_size) {
  for (int i = 0; i < array_size; ++i) std::cout << a[i] << " ";
  std::cout << "\n";
}

void Usage(std::string prog_name, int exponent) {
  std::cout << " Incorrect parameters\n";
  std::cout << " Usage: " << prog_name << " n k \n\n";
  std::cout << " n: Integer exponent presenting the size of the input array. "
               "The number of element in\n";
  std::cout << "    the array must be power of 2 (e.g., 1, 2, 4, ...). Please "
               "enter the corresponding\n";
  std::cout << "    exponent between 0 and " << exponent - 1 << ".\n";
  std::cout << " k: Seed used to generate a random sequence.\n";
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {
  int n, seed, size;
  int exp_max = log2(std::numeric_limits<int>::max());

  // Read parameters.
  try {
    n = std::stoi(argv[1]);

    // Verify the boundary of acceptance.
    if (n < 0 || n >= exp_max) {
      Usage(argv[0], exp_max);
      return -1;
    }

    seed = std::stoi(argv[2]);
    size = pow(2, n);
  } catch (...) {
    Usage(argv[0], exp_max);
    return -1;
  }

  std::cout << "\nArray size: " << size << ", seed: " << seed << "\n";

  size_t size_bytes = size * sizeof(int);

  // Memory allocated for host access only.
  int *data_cpu = (int *)malloc(size_bytes);

  // Memory allocated to store gpu results
  int *data_gpu = (int *)malloc(size_bytes);

  // Initialize the array randomly using a seed.
  srand(seed);

  for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
    data_gpu[i] = data_cpu[i] = rand() % 1000;
  }

  std::cout << "Bitonic sort (parallel)..\n";
  ParallelBitonicSort(data_gpu, n);

  std::cout << "Bitonic sort (serial)..\n";
  BitonicSort(data_cpu, n);

  // Verify
  int unequal = memcmp(data_gpu, data_cpu, size_bytes);
  std::cout << (unequal ? "FAIL" : "PASS") << std::endl;

  // Clean CPU memory.
  free(data_cpu);
  free(data_gpu);

  return 0;
}

//==============================================================
// Copyright © 2020 Intel Corporation
//
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
// =============================================================
//
// Bitonic Sort: this algorithm converts a randomized sequence of numbers into
// a bitonic sequence (two ordered sequences), and then merge these two ordered
// sequences into a ordered sequence. Bitonic sort algorithm is briefly
// described as followed:
//
// - First, it decomposes the randomized sequence of size 2**n into 2**(n-1)
// pairs where each pair consists of 2 consecutive elements. Note that each pair
// is a bitonic sequence.
// - Step 0: for each pair (sequence of size 2), the two elements are swapped so
// that the two consecutive pairs form  a bitonic sequence in increasing order,
// the next two pairs form the second bitonic sequence in decreasing order, the
// next two pairs form the third bitonic sequence in  increasing order, etc, ...
// . At the end of this step, we have 2**(n-1) bitonic sequences of size 2, and
// they follow an order increasing, decreasing, increasing, .., decreasing.
// Thus, they form 2**(n-2) bitonic sequences of size 4.
// - Step 1: for each new 2**(n-2) bitonic sequences of size 4, (each new
// sequence consists of 2 consecutive previous sequences), it swaps the elements
// so that at the end of step 1, we have 2**(n-2) bitonic sequences of size 4,
// and they follow an order: increasing, decreasing, increasing, ...,
// decreasing. Thus, they form 2**(n-3) bitonic sequences of size 8.
// - Same logic applies until we reach the last step.
// - Step n: at this last step, we have one bitonic sequence of size 2**n. The
// elements in the sequence are swapped until we have a sequence in increasing
// order.
//
// In this implementation, a randomized sequence of size 2**n is given (n is a
// positive number). At each stage, a part of step, the host redefines the
// ordered sequenes and sends data to the kernel. The kernel swaps the elements
// accordingly in parallel.
//
#include <math.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>
#include <limits>
#include <omp.h>

void ParallelBitonicSort(int input[], int n) {

  // n: the exponent used to set the array size. Array size = power(2, n)
  int size = pow(2, n);

  // step from 0, 1, 2, ...., n-1
  #pragma omp target data map(tofrom: input[0:size]) 
  {
    auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();

    for (int step = 0; step < n; step++) {
      // for each step s, stage goes s, s-1, ..., 0
      for (int stage = step; stage >= 0; stage--) {
        // In each state, construct a number (num_seq) of bitonic sequences of
        // size seq_len (2, 4, ...) num_seq stores the number of bitonic sequences
        // at each stage. seq_len stores the length of the bitonic sequence at
        // each stage.
        int seq_len = pow(2, stage + 1);
        // Constant used in the kernel: 2**(step-stage).
        int two_power = 1 << (step - stage);

        // Offload the work to kernel.
        #pragma omp target teams distribute parallel for thread_limit(256)
        for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
          // Assign the bitonic sequence number.
          int seq_num = i / seq_len;

          // Variable used to identified the swapped element.
          int swapped_ele = -1;

          // Because the elements in the first half in the bitonic
          // sequence may swap with elements in the second half,
          // only the first half of elements in each sequence is
          // required (seq_len/2).
          int h_len = seq_len / 2;

          if (i < (seq_len * seq_num) + h_len) swapped_ele = i + h_len;

          // Check whether increasing or decreasing order.
          int odd = seq_num / two_power;

          // Boolean variable used to determine "increasing" or
          // "decreasing" order.
          bool increasing = ((odd % 2) == 0);

          // Swap the elements in the bitonic sequence if needed
          if (swapped_ele != -1) {
            if (((input[i] > input[swapped_ele]) && increasing) ||
                ((input[i] < input[swapped_ele]) && !increasing)) {
              int temp = input[i];
              input[i] = input[swapped_ele];
              input[swapped_ele] = temp;
            }
          }
        }
      }  // end stage
    } // end step

    auto end = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    auto time = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::nanoseconds>(end - start).count();
    printf("Total kernel execution time: %f (ms)\n", time * 1e-6f);
  }
}

// Loop over the bitonic sequences at each stage in serial.
void SwapElements(int step, int stage, int num_sequence, int seq_len,
                  int *array) {
  for (int seq_num = 0; seq_num < num_sequence; seq_num++) {
    int odd = seq_num / (pow(2, (step - stage)));
    bool increasing = ((odd % 2) == 0);

    int h_len = seq_len / 2;

    // For all elements in a bitonic sequence, swap them if needed
    for (int i = seq_num * seq_len; i < seq_num * seq_len + h_len; i++) {
      int swapped_ele = i + h_len;

      if (((array[i] > array[swapped_ele]) && increasing) ||
          ((array[i] < array[swapped_ele]) && !increasing)) {
        int temp = array[i];
        array[i] = array[swapped_ele];
        array[swapped_ele] = temp;
      }
    }  // end for all elements in a sequence
  }    // end all sequences
}

// Function sorts an array in serial using bitonic sort algorithm. The size of
// the array is indicated by the exponent n: the array size is 2 ** n.
inline void BitonicSort(int a[], int n) {
  // n: the exponent indicating the array size = 2 ** n.

  // step from 0, 1, 2, ...., n-1
  for (int step = 0; step < n; step++) {
    // for each step s, stage goes s, s-1,..., 0
    for (int stage = step; stage >= 0; stage--) {
      // Sequences (same size) are formed at each stage.
      int num_sequence = pow(2, (n - stage - 1));
      // The length of the sequences (2, 4, ...).
      int sequence_len = pow(2, stage + 1);

      SwapElements(step, stage, num_sequence, sequence_len, a);
    }
  }
}

// Function showing the array.
void DisplayArray(int a[], int array_size) {
  for (int i = 0; i < array_size; ++i) std::cout << a[i] << " ";
  std::cout << "\n";
}

void Usage(std::string prog_name, int exponent) {
  std::cout << " Incorrect parameters\n";
  std::cout << " Usage: " << prog_name << " n k \n\n";
  std::cout << " n: Integer exponent presenting the size of the input array. "
               "The number of element in\n";
  std::cout << "    the array must be power of 2 (e.g., 1, 2, 4, ...). Please "
               "enter the corresponding\n";
  std::cout << "    exponent between 0 and " << exponent - 1 << ".\n";
  std::cout << " k: Seed used to generate a random sequence.\n";
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {
  int n, seed, size;
  int exp_max = log2(std::numeric_limits<int>::max());

  // Read parameters.
  try {
    n = std::stoi(argv[1]);

    // Verify the boundary of acceptance.
    if (n < 0 || n >= exp_max) {
      Usage(argv[0], exp_max);
      return -1;
    }

    seed = std::stoi(argv[2]);
    size = pow(2, n);
  } catch (...) {
    Usage(argv[0], exp_max);
    return -1;
  }

  std::cout << "\nArray size: " << size << ", seed: " << seed << "\n";

  size_t size_bytes = size * sizeof(int);

  // Memory allocated for host access only.
  int *data_cpu = (int *)malloc(size_bytes);

  // Memory allocated to store gpu results
  int *data_gpu = (int *)malloc(size_bytes);

  // Initialize the array randomly using a seed.
  srand(seed);

  for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
    data_gpu[i] = data_cpu[i] = rand() % 1000;
  }

  std::cout << "Bitonic sort (parallel)..\n";
  ParallelBitonicSort(data_gpu, n);

  std::cout << "Bitonic sort (serial)..\n";
  BitonicSort(data_cpu, n);

  // Verify
  int unequal = memcmp(data_gpu, data_cpu, size_bytes);
  std::cout << (unequal ? "FAIL" : "PASS") << std::endl;

  // Clean CPU memory.
  free(data_cpu);
  free(data_gpu);

  return 0;
}

prediction.fp32_flop_explanation: Looking at the SASS for the first invocation (step=0, stage=0): seq_len = 2^(0+1) = 2, two_power = 1<<(0-0) = 1. Each even thread i reads input[i] and input[i+1], which are consecutive pairs. Total unique read footprint = 33554432 × 4 bytes = 134217728 bytes (the entire array). The array is 2^25 × 4 = 128 MB, which is much larger than the 40 MB L2 cache. Each pair is read once (no reuse across threads), so DRAM reads ≈ 134217728 bytes. However, each pair of loads from an even thread touches at most 2 consecutive 4-byte ints (8 bytes), fitting in one or two 32-byte cache lines. The total unique footprint is 128 MB which exceeds L2, so essentially all reads go to DRAM: 134217728 bytes.
prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: For step=0, stage=0, the kernel swaps pairs where input[i] > input[i+1] (for even seq_num, increasing order) or input[i] < input[i+1] (for odd seq_num, decreasing order). With random data, roughly half of the 16777216 active threads will perform swaps, writing 2 × 4 = 8 bytes each. That's ~8388608 threads × 8 bytes = ~67108864 bytes. However, the writes are scattered across the full 128 MB array. Since the array far exceeds L2 (40 MB), and the write pattern is essentially random across the array with ~50% of cache lines being written, the written cache lines will be evicted to DRAM. With write-allocate policy, each 32-byte sector written also requires a read. The actual DRAM write traffic is approximately 67108864 bytes (the stores from ~half the active threads, 2 STG.E per swapping thread).

The first invocation corresponds to step=0, stage=0. The OpenMP runtime on clang for NVIDIA targets typically launches ceil(size / 256) = ceil(33554432 / 256) = 131072 teams. From the SASS, we see a grid-stride loop pattern (the outer loop at L_x_5 increments R12 by UR5 which is num_CTAs * 256). The runtime likely launches 131072 blocks (or possibly fewer with grid-stride), but the standard clang OpenMP behavior for this pattern is to launch ceil(N/blockSize) teams. Given size=33554432 and blockSize=256, gridSz.x = 131072.
prediction.blockSz_explanation: The pragma specifies thread_limit(256), and the SASS shows SHF.L.U32 R0, R12, 0x8, RZ which is R12 << 8 = R12 * 256, confirming 256 threads per block.
prediction.fp32_flop_explanation: Looking at the SASS, there are FP32 operations related to integer division emulation: I2F.RP (integer to float), MUFU.RCP (reciprocal), F2I.FTZ.U32.TRUNC.NTZ (float to int). These appear twice in the kernel body - once for computing seq_num = i / seq_len (around addresses 0x290-0x300) and once for computing odd = seq_num / two_power (around addresses 0x560-0x590). Each of these sequences has 1 I2F + 1 MUFU.RCP + 1 F2I = 3 FP32 ops per sequence. The first sequence (I2F at 0x290, MUFU.RCP at 0x2D0, F2I at 0x300) executes once per thread that enters the work region. The second sequence (I2F at 0x560, MUFU.RCP at 0x570, F2I at 0x590) only executes for threads where the condition at P0 is not taken (i.e., threads in the first half of each bitonic sequence). For step=0, stage=0: seq_len=2, so half the threads (16777216) do the swap path. First set: 33554432 threads × 3 FP32 ops = 100663296. Second set: 16777216 threads × 3 FP32 ops = 50331648. Total = 150994944. However, looking more carefully at the SASS flow: the first I2F/MUFU.RCP/F2I block is outside the inner loop and executes once per thread that passes the initial bounds check. The second block is inside the conditional path (only for threads where i < seq_len*seq_num + h_len). With 33554432 total threads and exactly half satisfying the condition: first block = 33554432 × 3 = 100663296, second block = 16777216 × 3 = 50331648. Total FP32 = 150994944.

prediction.dram_bytes_read_explanation: For step=0, stage=0: seq_len=2, h_len=1. Each even-indexed element (i where i < seq_len*seq_num + h_len, i.e., i % 2 == 0) reads input[i] and input[i+1] via two LDG.E instructions (4 bytes each). That's 16777216 threads doing 2 reads of 4 bytes = 134217728 bytes of unique read data. However, the total unique footprint is the entire array: 33554432 × 4 = 134217728 bytes. This is 128 MB, which far exceeds the 5 MB L2 cache, so essentially all reads go to DRAM. The two LDG.E loads per active thread read adjacent elements, so each active thread reads 8 bytes, but the unique footprint is 128 MB (every element is read once as input[i] by one thread and as input[swapped_ele] by another, but only half the threads do the loads). Total DRAM bytes read = 16777216 × 8 = 134217728 bytes.
prediction.dram_bytes_written_explanation: For step=0, stage=0: the swap only happens when elements are out of order. The array is randomly initialized with values 0-999. For the first step/stage, pairs of consecutive elements are compared and swapped if needed (alternating increasing/decreasing). Roughly half the pairs will need swapping. Each swap writes 2 elements × 4 bytes = 8 bytes via two STG.E instructions. With 16777216 pairs and roughly half needing swaps, about 8388608 pairs write 8 bytes each = 67108864 bytes. The total output footprint (up to 128 MB) far exceeds L2 cache (5 MB), so writes will spill to DRAM. However, the actual number of swaps depends on the random data. On average, for random data, about half the pairs are out of order, so approximately 67108864 bytes are written. But considering write-allocate behavior where even partial cache line writes cause full cache line traffic, and the scattered nature of writes (only some pairs swap), the DRAM write traffic is approximately 67108864 bytes.
